title: The Case For Data Centre Hyperloops
problem: Data movement at petabyte scale via optical networking takes weeks and consumes massive energy; for example, 30PB datasets require nearly a week to transfer at 400 Gbps while consuming megajoules just to operate the optical transceivers.
motivation: As ML, graph processing, and data analytics workloads scale to petabyte-sized datasets, network-based data transfer becomes a critical energy and latency bottleneck.
method: DHLs transport SSDs containing large datasets via magnetic levitation in low-pressure tubes through data centres, enabling speeds of hundreds of metres per second. This eliminates the network bandwidth and energy costs of data copying while providing terabyte-per-second access bandwidth and local latency once the data arrives.
key_novelty: Replacing network-based data copying with embodied physical transport of SSDs via magnetic levitation, exploiting SSD density improvements.
contributions: Proposes Data Centre Hyperloops (DHLs) using magnetic levitation to transport SSDs for large-scale data movement
Demonstrates 1.6x-376.1x energy reduction and 114.8x-646.4x speedup vs 400 Gbps optical networking
Models DHLs for ML training, physics experiments, and data backups, showing 5.7x-118x speedup (iso-power) for DLRM workloads
Provides cost analysis and engineering feasibility arguments for practical DHL deployment
limitations: Implementation challenges and architectural questions regarding real-world deployment are acknowledged but not fully addressed; paper frames itself as a call to action for future work.
primary_theme: Physical data transport via magnetic levitation for data centre interconnect
